Hi folks. Over the last month, I've been steering AI with the goal of proving and formalizing a proof of the following conjecture by John Conway from On Numbers and Games:

Concretely, using the Surreal definition from the CombinatorialGames library by @Violeta Hernández , I believe the above statement translates to:

import CombinatorialGames.Surreal.Multiplication

universe u

/-- Conway's definition: `x` is an omnific integer when it is
the cut with sole left option `x - 1` and sole right option `x + 1`. -/
abbrev IsConwayOmnificInteger (x : Surreal.{u}) : Prop :=
  x = !{{x - 1} | {x + 1}}' (by
    simp only [Set.mem_singleton_iff]
    rintro _ rfl _ rfl
    simp [sub_eq_add_neg])

/-- Conway's refinement conjecture: every equality `a * b = c * d` of
cut-defined omnific integers has an omnific refinement
`a = e * f`, `b = g * h`, `c = e * g`, `d = f * h`. -/
abbrev ConwayConjecture : Prop :=
  ∀ a b c d : Surreal.{u},
    IsConwayOmnificInteger a → IsConwayOmnificInteger b →
    IsConwayOmnificInteger c → IsConwayOmnificInteger d → a * b = c * d →
    ∃ e f g h : Surreal.{u},
      IsConwayOmnificInteger e ∧ IsConwayOmnificInteger f ∧
      IsConwayOmnificInteger g ∧ IsConwayOmnificInteger h ∧
      a = e * f ∧ b = g * h ∧ c = e * g ∧ d = f * h

To the best of my knowledge, the problem is not solved or formalized. I've published a candidate proof of the above statement at https://github.com/gaearon/conway-refinement. I would appreciate any eyes on it and any comments about what might be wrong about it.

A few quick points from README:

  • There's also a proven Mathlib-only ~250 line version of the statement.
  • Proof for both statements report [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound].
  • There's a project-wide linter forbidding the use of other axioms, taken from TauCeti.
  • The proof was entirely written by AI under my steering for a month
  • All of my steering was non-mathematical (I was feeding it papers, recognizing stalls and misdirections, experimenting with the harnesses, and managing engineering work)
  • Since the proof may have ended up more complicated than needed, I've built some custom tooling to make it more legible to mathematicians:
    • Some results can get marked with a special annotation in Lean source code
    • They get bundled into a website along with AI-generated prose
    • The website includes "proof maps" for every such result (example)
    • Each result also includes a readonly Lean proof state for every caret position that you can explore by hovering or moving the cursor (example)

My goal with the project was partially to prove the conjecture, and partially to have some fun and see how far I can take it without actually understanding the field. Obviously, I was very limited with what I can do with no mathematical intuition, and I'm very curious whether anything from my workflow would have been useful to mathematicians.

I tried to get some feedback from mathematicians working in the area, and some subset of the proof seemed to check out, but LLM prose was very difficult to understand. That is in part why I've rebuilt the presentation around these Lean "proof maps", as I hope they'll help make AI's argument more legible and hopefully compress it down in the future.


I would be grateful for any feedback, and most of all for a debunking of the result.

Thanks!

Some superficial comments on the presentation based on a very quick skim of the website:

  • This would be much easier (for this human) to read if there was some glue text between the statements of theorems and if there were fleshed-out introductions to each of the chapters explaining where things are going and giving motivation for the results that follow. Maybe tastes vary here.
  • There is a chapter with a list of references, but none of the earlier chapters seem to cite any of them (perhaps I missed them?). I took a quick peek at some of the Lean code and it does look like there are some more precise citations there, which is good, but such attributions should probably be included in the web version as well. (Apologies again if I missed them)
    • Either way, some easy-to-find text that explains which results are original to this project and which come from previous work would be helpful in figuring where the key new ideas are.
  • Have you seen verso-blueprint? It's a Lean FRO-developed library which can also be used for making expository websites from Lean projects. The style of the reference blueprints there might give you a sense of what I mean by "glue" in my first bullet point.

Using cancellativity it can be seen that the statement is equivalent to that the ring of omnific integers is a docs#DecompositionMonoid.
Coincidentally Joel David Hamkins has recently written about unique factorization in NatOrdinal, a subring of the omnific integers.

Totally agree! I've written about the process a bit in the README but basically I only understand the statement, and pretty much none of the proof. The proof was entirely AI-driven, and my role was more akin to a engineering manager with no domain expertise.

In particular, this means that I can't actually tell what the "glue" between the theorems is, and what the chapters actually say. I could perhaps have AI summarize them and find that glue.

I didn't risk it for the initial presentation because previously I had the opposite problem. I was trying to generate a traditional "paper" style argument with connective tissue from the Lean proof, and the feedback from the mathematicians was that it was very difficult to follow because the model kept trying to invent its own inconsistent terminology, or made inferences that didn't make sense.

This is why I've thrown out the "paper" completely and instead had AI pick out the most "important" nodes in the Lean proof graph, and annotate them with short prose proofs one by one. Then I built the tooling (forked from Verso btw :) to visualize the graph between those nodes, asking AI to select more nodes until it felt that the graph didn't have too many unexplained jumps. When the AI was relatively happy with the graph completeness, I've had it cluster the selected nodes into consecutive "zones" so that they could tell a sort of linear narrative with some occasional forks.

So I lost all the glue, but at least I hope now there's fewer hallucinations, though it would definitely be cool to try to get a high level picture again. Maybe AI can write the glue better now that each node is more precise than when it attempted to summarize the entire Lean proof. It's definitely worth trying.

There was a lot of manual steering. I'll probably write up a blog post at some point. In general the workflow was to try to make incremental progress towards the conjecture (or some less ambitious part of it), capture supposedly new mathematics, do adversarial reviews, incorporate stuff that survives into a giant document. Then repeatedly tell fresh agents to burn the document down unless there's something they really want to salvage. Then at some point when we got partial result (finite degree primality), I started a concerted effort to formalize pieces of main prerequisite papers (Berarducci and LM24) into Lean and try to make progress towards certifying that smaller result. While that's ongoing, in parallel, again try to move forward purely "on paper".

"Burn everything down" cycles were at least as important as "try to find new directions". In general it seems like the workflow is to explore a bunch of directions, capture any interesting partial results, and when there's enough to push for a clear subresult, try to get confidence on it and then formalize in Lean. Then repeat.

Really, the biggest thing was to learn to spot when models are starting to bullshit or go in circles or give up. The last step towards resolving the conjecture was literally me saying something like "you can do it, re-read all sources again to see if some existing technique helps" to an agent that gave up.

And without doubt, having a stack of papers locally in .tex was super helpful for them to actually understand what we're working with.

It seems to me that the most valuable thing that has been proven here, mathematically speaking, is Corollary 168. The result about omnific integers should be a one-liner away from this, and the fact that it isn't is really a deficiency of my own combinatorial games library. I have a good amount of code written about omnific integers and Hahn series that hasn't yet been pushed to master -- we're in dire need of reviewers!

The fact that this result is so closely tied up to Hahn series means that I'm probably not the best person to review it... Well, this is somewhat of a farfetched ask, but I think there are other conjectures within CGT which might be within the reach of AI (or really, any intelligent and dedicated expert). Here's two that are of personal interest.

Multiplication as a subshuffle. Every surreal number can be associated to a sequence of signs (+, -) with transfinite length. Let x, y be two surreals, whose sign sequences have lengths α, β. You can create an α × β grid by multiplying all of the pairs of signs together. The conjecture (Gonshor 1970, p. 110) is that you can find a path through this grid that spells out the sign sequence of xy; the only restriction is that this path is injective, and that if (i₁, j₁), (i₂, j₂) are in the path with i₁ ≤ i₂ and j₁ ≤ j₂, then (i₂, j₂) must be later in the path than (i₁, j₁).

There is a known procedure to compute the sign sequence of a product (Gonshor 1970, Theorem 5.12), but it's very tedious. I'm not aware of any progress on this subshuffle conjecture, so even testing it on e.g. dyadic rationals or powers of ω would be nice. This conjecture would imply a separate open problem, which is that the birthday of the product of two surreal numbers is bounded by the Hessenberg product of their birthdays. I believe (Ehrlich & van den Dries, 2001) is the state of the art here.

Algebraically closed nimbers. Conway proves that the set of nimbers below ω^ω^ω forms an algebraically closed field. Finding the next largest nimber with this property has remained an open problem. Really, we don't understand all that much about the nimbers after. Conway figured out the general structure of nimbers up to ε₀, and a very recent paper by Lucia Risnoveanu extends this to ε_(ω^ω^ω). But that's as far as we've gotten. In the opposite direction, an unpublished manuscript by a friend (which I can send, if you're interested) shows that all nimbers of the form φ(x@ω) for x > 0, in the notation of Veblen's multivariate function are algebraically closed.
Also, if you can ask your AI this. What parts of the formalization are new, and which parts are just formalizing the referenced papers? It seems to me that the latter is a pretty big percentage.

In terms of Lean lines of code, I'd expect a very sizable chunk to be LM24 and Berarducci. (In an earlier version I actually grouped by paper but it seemed customary in Lean repos to group by math object so I had it redo the folder layout.)

In terms of actual proof, I believe the parts not explicitly marked as e.g. "LM24" or "Ber00" etc in https://gaearon.github.io/conway-refinement/blueprint.pdf or in the proof map to be either well-known general facts (for some basic claims), or actually new (or at least not explicitly taken from these sources, but possibly known in other contexts). I'll recheck that later.

In particular, my impression is that https://gaearon.github.io/conway-refinement/#/map/hahn-series-polynomial-algebra was not known to be true before, and so the same applies to whatever's downstream from it. There could be a shorter way to it though.

Just finished reading (mostly skimming) Berarducci (2000), from the references. I think we've collectively learned over the past few days that ideas are just as if not more important than the proof certificates, so I thought I'd share what I learned.

He considers the ideal J of the ring K⟦G^≤0⟧, generated by all monomials t^r with r < 0. He calls the quotient K⟦G^≤0⟧/J the "germs" of the series; the idea is that an element here depends only on the powers t^r for r "close enough" to 0.

He defines a function v_J : K⟦G^≤0⟧ → On which he calls the ordinal value. It's characterized by:

  • v_J(b) = 0 for b ∈ J
  • v_J(b + k) = 1 for b ∈ J and k ∈ K nonzero
  • v_J(b + k) = the least order type of the support of c ≡ b mod J otherwise

The value of v_J is always an additive principal ordinal. The main theorem of the paper is that for G = ℝ, and in particular for G Archimedean, the value v_J is multiplicative, when the ordinals are endowed with natural multiplication. As a corollary, the ideal J is prime.

He then uses this to prove the existence of irreducible elements in K⟦ℝ^≤0⟧. Specifically, he shows that if b ∉ J has an order type ≥ ω which is multiplicative principal, then b and b + 1 are irreducible. With the idea being that if it decomposed as the product of two factors, then one of them has v_J = 1, which is not too difficult to discard.

The paper leaves open whether v_J is multiplicative for a general G. I would guess this gets tackled in later papers in the references. I'm still not clear on how exactly the ordinal value gets used in the refinement proof, either, though chapter 2 of the blueprint is basically just all of the results I just listed.

Ah, Pitteloud (2002) proves that the multiplicativity property is false in general :frown:

What that paper does is find a new lower bound for v_J, which Pitteloud uses to prove that J is a prime ideal for any dense ordered group G. He also proves under the same assumption that every element in K⟦G^≤0⟧/J not in K admits a (not necessarily unique) factorization into irreducibles.

I've kept digging through the references. The 2006 and 2017 papers seem to mostly be small improvements over the previous work. Really, it's "A factorisation theory for generalised power series and omnific integers" from 2024 that seems to contain most of the meat; in its first section it already summarizes the main ideas from the previous referenced papers, and presents the state of the art regarding the factorization of Hahn series. It's an 80 page paper, so I think I'll spent the next few days mulling over it. I suspect that whatever ideas don't appear here (i.e. the construction of the Cantor-Bendixson value, or the isomorphism of Hahn series with polynomial rings of formal power series) are likely the AI's own.

Also, if you can ask your AI this. What parts of the formalization are new, and which parts are just formalizing the referenced papers? It seems to me that the latter is a pretty big percentage.

Here's what it says on that:

Relative to the literature actually checked in the project, the strongest apparent new results are:

• finite-degree primality for real-exponent nonpositive Hahn series;

• polynomiality of the full principal ring in every ordinal degree, especially the limit-degree syzygy-integration argument;

• the resulting full primality theorem for real-exponent Hahn series;
• multiplicativity and polynomial germ theory for the intrinsic Cantor--Bendixson rank over the general exponent groups needed at surreal tails;
• arbitrary-cofinality shell correction on exact-rank sets;
• equation-specific common-tail localization and occupied-class rank induction giving Conway refinement.

The standard notions of primality and refinement, surreal normal forms, Berarducci's real-exponent order value, LM24 factorization and the published low-degree germ results are inputs.

I wrote a blog post about the process: https://overreacted.io/how-i-vibed-a-proof-of-conways-conjecture/

It's light on mathematical detail (which I can't easily evaluate) but tells the rough progression towards the proof, and what worked / didn't work.
